quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Login Problems] Following last week's password reset, some users may still be unable to log in. We are aware of this and are working on it. In the meantime, please do not try more than three times, as this will lock your account.
quests.question: What is IT's position on the login problem?
options: The problem affects only users who have tried to log in more than three times.
IT has not yet fixed the underlying problem.
IT expects the problem to disappear once the locked accounts are unlocked.
The password reset failed because users typed their passwords wrongly.
quests.correctAnswer: IT has not yet fixed the underlying problem.
quests.hint: Read what IT says it is doing, and what it asks users to do "in the meantime."
quests.explanation: "Working on it" and "in the meantime" show the fault is still there. The warning about locking is a stopgap.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Budget Item] Minutes, 12 May: Yusuf to circulate the budget by Friday. Minutes, 28 April: Yusuf to circulate the budget by the 14th. Minutes, 31 March: budget to be discussed.
quests.question: What do the three sets of minutes show?
options: The budget was discussed in March, and the date has been fixed ever since.
The committee has changed who is responsible for the budget.
Yusuf has finished the budget and is waiting for it to be approved.
The budget task has been postponed more than once.
quests.correctAnswer: The budget task has been postponed more than once.
quests.hint: Compare the same action across the three sets of minutes.
quests.explanation: The same task appears with a new deadline each time. That shows it has slipped repeatedly.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Short-Staffed] Notice on the shop door: "Our team are happy to help. Please be patient. We are short-staffed and, like you, we would rather be at home."
quests.question: What is the shop asking of customers?
options: Customers may face delays, and the writer hopes for understanding.
The shop is closing early because the staff want to go home.
The shop is asking customers to help by serving themselves.
The manager is apologising for poor service in the past.
quests.correctAnswer: Customers may face delays, and the writer hopes for understanding.
quests.hint: Which phrases explain the situation and which ask for something?
quests.explanation: "Short-staffed" explains possible waiting, and "please be patient" asks for tolerance. The joke about home is meant to soften the message.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Alder Lane] Water main repairs on Alder Lane will run from 9 to 12 March. The road will be closed to through traffic, with access for residents only. Buses on route 14 will be diverted via Mill Street.
quests.question: How does the closure affect people who live on Alder Lane?
options: They will still be able to drive to their homes.
They must park outside the lane and walk in.
They can use route 14 buses directly to their door.
They will have no water on any of the repair days.
quests.correctAnswer: They will still be able to drive to their homes.
quests.hint: Which phrase distinguishes residents from other drivers?
quests.explanation: "Closed to through traffic" with "access for residents only" means people who live on the lane can still enter.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Swimming Not Advised] Water quality: swimming is not advised today. Test results are expected tomorrow. Dogs must be kept on leads on the beach at all times.
quests.question: How certain are the authorities about the water?
options: The beach will be closed to dogs until the results arrive.
The authorities are not yet sure that the water is safe.
The water is polluted and will be tested to find the cause.
Swimming is banned every year on days when dogs are on the beach.
quests.correctAnswer: The authorities are not yet sure that the water is safe.
quests.hint: What are the authorities waiting for?
quests.explanation: "Not advised" until results arrive shows that they are cautious and waiting to confirm.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Story Time] Because of a burst pipe, the children's section is closed until further notice. Story time will be held in the reading room. Please do not bring buggies into the reading room.
quests.question: What is the reading room like?
options: It is quieter than the children's section.
It has been damaged by the burst pipe as well.
It is far from the entrance, so buggies are difficult to move.
It has limited space.
quests.correctAnswer: It has limited space.
quests.hint: Why would a library ask people to leave buggies out?
quests.explanation: Asking for no buggies suggests space is tight, especially with story time visitors added.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Your Patience] Dear Mr. Kaya, thank you for your patience. Your refund has been approved and will be processed within 5 to 10 working days. We are unable to give an exact date.
quests.question: What does the thanks for patience suggest?
options: The company has decided to refund only part of the amount.
Mr. Kaya has already waited a long time.
Mr. Kaya asked the company to delay the refund.
Mr. Kaya has made a mistake on his refund form.
quests.correctAnswer: Mr. Kaya has already waited a long time.
quests.hint: What does the first sentence suggest about the past?
quests.explanation: Thanking someone for patience implies a delay. The vague timeframe adds to that.
clueWords: unable to give an exact date

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Generic Reply] Thank you for your feedback. We are sorry your experience did not meet your expectations. We have shared your comments with the team. Management. (This reply appears under each of the hotel's last twelve one-star reviews.)
quests.question: What kind of reply is this?
options: It promises a refund to every guest who wrote a one-star review.
It is a standard reply that offers no specific action.
It is written only for guests who complained about the same problem.
It shows that the hotel investigates each complaint separately.
quests.correctAnswer: It is a standard reply that offers no specific action.
quests.hint: What does the note in brackets reveal?
quests.explanation: The same wording under twelve reviews shows it is generic, and it promises no action beyond "sharing."

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Everything Okay] "Everything okay with your meal?" the waiter asked, already turning toward the next table. "Yes, fine," said the customer, whose plate was still nearly full.
quests.question: What does the customer's full plate reveal?
options: The customer is waiting for the waiter to bring a different dish.
The customer is probably too full to finish after a large starter.
The customer is not satisfied but did not say so.
The customer would like the waiter to take the plate away.
quests.correctAnswer: The customer is not satisfied but did not say so.
quests.hint: Compare what the customer says with the plate.
quests.explanation: The customer's words are polite, but a nearly full plate contradicts them. The waiter's turned body also invites a quick answer.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Twenty Minutes] The textbook says each exercise "should take about twenty minutes." At the pilot school, students took an average of forty-five.
quests.question: What do the two time figures suggest about the estimate?
options: The exercises at the pilot school were harder than those in the textbook.
The pilot school's students were unusually slow readers.
The textbook's authors tested the exercises with older students.
The textbook's estimate is too low for typical students.
quests.correctAnswer: The textbook's estimate is too low for typical students.
quests.hint: Compare the estimate with the average time.
quests.explanation: Forty-five minutes is more than double twenty. This suggests the textbook underestimated the time.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Broadly Stable] The exam board said this year's pass rate had "remained broadly stable." The figure was 71 percent, against 74 percent last year.
quests.question: How does the board's wording compare with the figures?
options: It shows that the exam was easier this year.
It downplays a small fall.
It hides a large fall in the pass rate.
It correctly reports that the pass rate has not changed.
quests.correctAnswer: It downplays a small fall.
quests.hint: Compare the two percentages with the word "stable."
quests.explanation: A fall of three points is small but real. "Broadly stable" plays down the difference.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Thirty Minutes] The new homework policy limits tasks to 30 minutes. Teachers say they are finding it "hard to cover the syllabus." Some parents report their children are now "getting on with projects on their own."
quests.question: How has the homework limit affected different groups?
options: The limit has improved results because teachers now set better tasks.
The limit has helped teachers cover the syllabus but has upset parents.
The limit has reduced projects because parents want more homework.
The limit has eased pressure on students but made planning harder for teachers.
quests.correctAnswer: The limit has eased pressure on students but made planning harder for teachers.
quests.hint: What do teachers report, and what do some parents report?
quests.explanation: Teachers say coverage is difficult, and parents report a positive effect on their children. So the policy has different effects for different groups.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Swifts] Scientists tracked thirty swifts fitted with tiny sensors. The birds flew for months without landing, and the sensors recorded almost no rest. The researchers suspect the birds doze briefly while gliding.
quests.question: How certain is the claim about sleep?
options: It is a suspicion, not something the sensors confirmed.
It applies only to swifts that landed during the study.
It is based on other researchers' observations of gliding birds.
It has been proved by the sensors recording short periods of sleep.
quests.correctAnswer: It is a suspicion, not something the sensors confirmed.
quests.hint: Which verb does the passage use for the sleep idea?
quests.explanation: "Suspect" shows a possibility. The sensors recorded almost no rest, so they could not confirm sleep.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Glacier Sign] A sign on the path reads "Glacier edge, 1995." Today the ice edge lies about 200 metres uphill, beyond a fence.
quests.question: What does the position of the sign show?
options: The fence was built to keep walkers off the ice.
The glacier has shrunk since 1995.
The sign was placed by scientists to show where the edge will be in the future.
The glacier moved uphill after 1995.
quests.correctAnswer: The glacier has shrunk since 1995.
quests.hint: Where was the edge in 1995, and where is it now?
quests.explanation: The sign marks the old edge, and the current edge is uphill. The ice has retreated.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Scent Trail] When a scout ant finds food, it returns to the nest leaving a scent trail, and other ants follow. If the food runs out, the trail fades within hours, since no ants renew it.
quests.question: Why do ants stop following the trail?
options: Ants stop following a trail once the scent is no longer renewed.
Ants stop following the trail because the scout ant has left the nest.
Ants follow a trail for as long as the food remains in view.
Ants lose the trail when other ants remove the scent on purpose.
quests.correctAnswer: Ants stop following a trail once the scent is no longer renewed.
quests.hint: What does the trail need in order to stay strong?
quests.explanation: The trail lasts only while ants keep adding to it. When they stop because the food is gone, it fades.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Smart Battery] The update adds a "smart battery" mode. Early testers say background apps are closed more often. One writes: "Great, except my alarm did not go off on Tuesday."
quests.question: What may explain the missed alarm?
options: The update changed the alarm volume, so the tester slept through it.
The alarm app was removed by the update.
The new mode may have closed the alarm app.
The alarm was set for the wrong time before the update.
quests.correctAnswer: The new mode may have closed the alarm app.
quests.hint: Connect the feature to the tester's problem.
quests.explanation: If apps are closed more often, an alarm app may be closed too. The tester's "except" links the feature to the failure.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Two-Step Login] After the company introduced two-step login, hacked accounts fell by 60 percent. Customer complaints about being "locked out" doubled.
quests.question: What trade-off did two-step login bring?
options: Security improved, but many users found logging in harder.
Security improved, but hackers found new ways to enter.
Security improved, and customers were pleased with the new login.
Customers were locked out because the system was hacked.
quests.correctAnswer: Security improved, but many users found logging in harder.
quests.hint: Read both statistics.
quests.explanation: Fewer hacked accounts shows a gain. Doubled lock-out complaints shows a cost. It has a benefit and a price.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Place Names] The voice assistant answers most questions correctly. In the test it misunderstood every question that contained a regional place name. The company says it "will improve."
quests.question: Why does the assistant fail the test?
options: It cannot answer questions about geography.
It cannot understand people who speak with a regional accent.
It answers slowly whenever a question is more than five words long.
It has trouble with names it has not been trained on.
quests.correctAnswer: It has trouble with names it has not been trained on.
quests.hint: What did all the failed questions have in common?
quests.explanation: All failures included regional place names. That pattern points to a gap in what the assistant knows.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Return Not Received] We have not received your tax return for last year. If you have already sent it, please disregard this letter. If not, a $100 penalty will be added on the 31st.
quests.question: Why was the letter sent?
options: It was sent only to people who have already paid the penalty.
It was sent to everyone without a return on record, whether or not they had sent one.
It was sent because the return contained a mistake.
It was sent to everyone who filed late last year.
quests.correctAnswer: It was sent to everyone without a return on record, whether or not they had sent one.
quests.hint: Which sentence allows for the reader's return being already sent?
quests.explanation: The letter says "if you have already sent it," so the department is not sure whether the return is missing or just not recorded.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Lunch-Box Habit] Aisha's monthly spending on takeaways fell from $180 to $60 after she began bringing lunch to work. Her grocery bill rose by $45.
quests.question: How much is Aisha saving?
options: She is saving $60 a month, which is what she now spends on takeaways.
She is spending more than before because groceries cost more.
She is saving money overall, but less than the drop in takeaway spending suggests.
She is saving $180 a month by bringing lunch.
quests.correctAnswer: She is saving money overall, but less than the drop in takeaway spending suggests.
quests.hint: Balance the fall against the rise.
quests.explanation: She saves $120 on takeaways and spends $45 more on groceries, so her net saving is smaller than $120.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Simplified Fees] The bank will "simplify" its fees from 1 May. The monthly charge falls from $9 to $7. Withdrawals at other banks' machines, until now free, will cost $2.50 each.
quests.question: Who might lose out under the new fees?
options: The bank is adding a fee that only new customers will pay.
The bank will lose money from customers who use its own machines.
Some customers will end up paying more.
Every customer will pay less because the monthly charge falls.
quests.correctAnswer: Some customers will end up paying more.
quests.hint: Who would gain from the lower monthly charge, and who would lose?
quests.explanation: The lower charge saves $2 a month, but a customer who withdraws at other machines even once will pay more.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Weather Permitting] The 4:30 ferry is "subject to weather." The website adds that in high winds crossings are cancelled without notice, and that tickets for cancelled sailings can be exchanged but not refunded.
quests.question: What risk do travellers face?
options: They will always be told of a cancellation the day before.
They should book the 4:30 ferry because it is unaffected by weather.
They can claim a refund if wind stops the ferry.
They risk a last-minute cancellation with limited compensation.
quests.correctAnswer: They risk a last-minute cancellation with limited compensation.
quests.hint: What is offered for a cancelled sailing, and what is not?
quests.explanation: Cancellation can occur without notice, and passengers can only exchange tickets. They cannot recover the money.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Short Walk] The hotel is described as "a short walk from the beach." Guests' photos on the review site show a steep hill and a busy road between the two.
quests.question: What do guests' photos suggest about the description?
options: "Short walk" may understate the effort involved.
Guests prefer the hill because of the view.
The hotel is on the beach, and the photos show only the road.
The walk is short, but the road is closed to walkers.
quests.correctAnswer: "Short walk" may understate the effort involved.
quests.hint: What do guests' photos show that the description does not?
quests.explanation: The description sounds easy, but the photos show a hill and a road. The description leaves out difficulties.
clueWords: a short walk from the beach

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [The 9:24] Off-peak tickets are valid on trains departing after 9:30. If you board earlier, you must pay the difference to the conductor. Passengers on the 9:24 to Leeds, please note.
quests.question: What should passengers on the 9:24 infer?
options: Their off-peak tickets will not be valid without extra payment.
The conductor will let passengers travel without paying the difference.
Passengers must change to a later train to use off-peak tickets.
The 9:24 will be delayed until 9:30 so that the tickets are valid.
quests.correctAnswer: Their off-peak tickets will not be valid without extra payment.
quests.hint: Compare the departure time with the validity time.
quests.explanation: The 9:24 leaves before 9:30, so an off-peak ticket does not cover it.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Crossing Petition] Residents of Elm Road collected 212 signatures asking for a crossing outside the school. The council replied that traffic counts "do not currently justify" one. A parent said, "They will count when somebody gets hurt."
quests.question: What does the parent's comment imply?
options: She is warning that the road will be dangerous once the school is open.
She believes the council has already counted the traffic correctly.
She believes the council will act only after an accident.
She thinks the council has ignored the parents' petition entirely.
quests.correctAnswer: She believes the council will act only after an accident.
quests.hint: What does "They will count" refer to?
quests.explanation: The parent's remark is sarcastic. She suggests that the council waits for evidence of harm before acting.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [River Clean-Up] Volunteers filled forty bags at the river clean-up. Organisers noted that the same stretch had been cleaned only three months ago.
quests.question: What does the amount collected suggest?
options: The volunteers did not clean the stretch properly three months ago.
The volunteers filled more bags than in previous years.
The river carries litter from other towns to that stretch.
Litter builds up quickly on that stretch.
quests.correctAnswer: Litter builds up quickly on that stretch.
quests.hint: Compare the amount collected with the time since the last clean.
quests.explanation: Forty bags in three months means the problem returns quickly.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Costings] Cllr Hart proposed a tree-planting scheme. Cllr Bell said he "fully supports the principle" but asked for further costings. The vote was postponed.
quests.question: How firmly does Cllr Bell support the scheme?
options: He opposes tree planting but does not want to say so.
He wants to change the scheme so that it costs less.
His support is conditional and he is hesitant to commit.
He has already voted in favour and wants to see the figures afterwards.
quests.correctAnswer: His support is conditional and he is hesitant to commit.
quests.hint: What does "but" add to "fully supports the principle"?
quests.explanation: Supporting a principle while asking for costings signals that he will not vote yes until the details are settled.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Up from What] Every year the town spends more on the summer festival, and every year the organisers say attendance is "up." Nobody asks "up from what?" or whether the shops on the high street see any benefit.
quests.question: What is the writer's position?
options: He thinks the organisers deserve credit for increasing attendance.
He believes the festival should receive less money than the shops.
He doubts that the festival's benefits justify the spending.
He is certain that attendance has fallen every year.
quests.correctAnswer: He doubts that the festival's benefits justify the spending.
quests.hint: What questions does the writer say nobody asks?
quests.explanation: The writer raises the missing baseline and the benefit to shops. These questions imply doubt.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Not Reading] Your article says young people do not read. In my classes they read constantly: messages, forums, subtitles. What they do not do is read what I set. That is a different problem.
quests.question: Who is the writer, and what does she think?
options: She is a parent who believes teenagers read too little at home.
She is a student who thinks the article is unfair to young people.
She is a librarian who wants young people to read more novels.
She is a teacher who thinks the article misdescribes the issue.
quests.correctAnswer: She is a teacher who thinks the article misdescribes the issue.
quests.hint: What distinction does the writer make?
quests.explanation: She separates not reading at all from not reading assigned texts. Her reference to "my classes" shows she is a teacher.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [The Comparison] Commuters complain about the price of train tickets, but rarely mention that the same journey by car costs more once parking is included. I am not saying fares are fair. I am saying the comparison is rarely made.
quests.question: What point is the writer making about fares?
options: He thinks complaints overlook a relevant comparison, without defending the fares.
He thinks train fares are fair because driving is expensive.
He thinks commuters should drive because parking costs less than tickets.
He thinks complaints about fares are exaggerated by newspapers.
quests.correctAnswer: He thinks complaints overlook a relevant comparison, without defending the fares.
quests.hint: What two statements does the writer separate?
quests.explanation: He says he is not defending the fares, only pointing out an omitted comparison. His argument is about incomplete complaints.
